species.name: Aldrovanda vesiculosa
species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Droseraceae - Genus Aldrovanda - Subgenus Aldrovanda - Section Aldrovanda
species.typeLocality: Bologna, Budrio, IT, Amadeus fide D.Monti s.n. (LINN 397.1) Walters
species.summary: A rootless aquatic snap trap that floats in whorls and snaps shut on tiny water fleas.
species.description: Aldrovanda vesiculosa is a free-floating aquatic carnivore with whorls of leaves that resemble the paddles of a waterwheel. Each leaf ends in a small, translucent snap trap with trigger hairs. The plant has no roots and survives winter as a turion. Once widespread across the Old World, it is now rare and threatened throughout much of its range.
species.etymology: Aldrovanda honours Ulisse Aldrovandi, an Italian naturalist; vesiculosa means 'with small bladders'.
species.careGroupTagline: Float, submerge and let the bladders hunt.
species.careNotes: Soft, acidic water, strong light and a cool winter rest. It is a specialist plant and not recommended for beginners.

photo.alt: Photograph of Aldrovanda vesiculosa

species.conservationNote: Widely declining and locally extinct across much of its former range; wetland conservation is essential.
species.nativeRange: Widespread across Africa, Asia, Europe, Oceania (37 countries/territories)

species.name: Cephalotus follicularis
species.classification: Subclass Rosidae - Order Oxalidales - Family Cephalotaceae - Genus Cephalotus - Subgenus Cephalotus - Section Cephalotus
species.typeLocality: Van Leuwin Land, Esperance Bay, W.A., AU, 1792, J.Labillardiere s.n./Leschenault (G00176809)
species.summary: A small, reptilian pitcher from Western Australia with a toothed rim and a domed lid.
species.description: Cephalotus follicularis is the sole member of its family and one of the most distinctive carnivorous plants. It produces two kinds of leaves: flat, ordinary leaves and modified pitcher leaves with a toothed peristome and a lid. The pitchers are small but beautifully patterned in green, red and purple. It grows in peaty swamps near Albany in Western Australia and is highly sought after by collectors.
species.etymology: Cephalotus comes from the Greek kephale ('head'), referring to the head-like anthers; follicularis means 'with small bags' or 'follicles'.
species.discoveredBy: Collected in Western Australia in 1801 and described by Jacques Labillardière in 1806.

species.description: Craniolaria annua is a member of the craniolaria genus Craniolaria (family Martyniaceae). Craniolaria is a small genus of sticky-leaved annuals in the Martyniaceae. The leaves and stems are covered with glandular hairs that trap small insects, but the plants are not as strongly carnivorous as Drosera or Pinguicula. It was described by L. in 1753. The ICPS snapshot records it from Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Haiti, Puerto Rico, Venezuela. The type locality is Ehret, Pl.Papil.Rar.:tab.1, f.2 (1748) Barrie.

species.summary: A hooded, cobra-shaped pitcher that needs cool, flowing water and a cool root run.
species.description: Darlingtonia californica is a striking pitcher plant from the cold seeps of northern California and south-western Oregon. Its tubular leaves arch over into a hooded head with a forked appendage that resembles a snake's tongue. Insects enter through openings beneath the hood and are guided down into the pitcher. The plant depends on cool, flowing water and is challenging to grow in warm climates.
species.etymology: Darlingtonia honours William Darlington, an American botanist; californica refers to California.
species.discoveredBy: Discovered by William D. Brackenridge during the Wilkes Expedition in 1841 and described by John Torrey in 1853.

species.typeLocality: icon in Ellis mss. Note book 3:25r (LINN) E.C.Nelson
species.summary: The world's most famous snap trap: two hinged lobes, three trigger hairs on each lobe, and a lightning-fast closing mechanism.
species.description: Dionaea muscipula forms a rosette of leaves whose broad petioles end in paired, jaw-like lobes. Each lobe carries three sensitive trigger hairs; two touches within about twenty seconds cause the trap to snap shut, and further stimulation begins digestion. The trap is a highly modified leaf, not a flower, and the plant uses it to supplement the nutrients it cannot get from its poor, acidic soil. In the wild it is confined to a small part of the Carolinas, where it grows in wet pine savanna that depends on periodic fire.
species.etymology: Dionaea honours Dione, a Greek goddess associated with Aphrodite; muscipula means 'mouse trap'.
species.discoveredBy: Brought to European attention by Governor Arthur Dobbs in the 1750s and described in John Ellis's 1768 account, with the name attributed to Daniel Solander.

species.summary: Dioncophyllum thollonii is a sticky leaves (borderline) carnivore from Congo, Gabon, described by Baill. in 1890.
species.description: Dioncophyllum thollonii is a member of the dioncophyllum genus Dioncophyllum (family Dioncophyllaceae). Dioncophyllum thollonii is a tropical liana in the Dioncophyllaceae, a family that also contains the famous Triphyophyllum. Its leaves bear glandular structures and the plant has been discussed as a possible proto-carnivore, but it is not a practical cultivated carnivore. It was described by Baill. in 1890. The ICPS snapshot records it from Congo, Gabon. The type locality is Niari Distr., Comba near Mindouli 105 km W Brazzaville, CG, 6. 1888, Thollon 975 (P).
species.careNotes: No specialist care group is assigned. Follow the Dioncophyllum genus care sheet and adjust for the species' native climate.

species.typeLocality: Cape, ZA, R.Hamet 2842 (P00064805)
species.summary: A neat, clump-forming rosette with spoon-shaped leaves and a generous display of dew.
species.description: Drosera aliciae forms tight rosettes of wedge-shaped leaves that are densely covered with red-tipped glands. It is native to the Cape and grows in wet, sandy seeps. Mature plants produce offsets and can form impressive clumps. The small pink flowers are produced on tall scapes and the plant self-seeds readily.
species.etymology: Named for Alice, a name associated with the plant's discoverer or a botanical patron; the original dedication is not fully documented.
species.careGroupTagline: Forgiving, frost-sensitive and happy in a bright window.
species.careNotes: A very forgiving sundew for a bright windowsill or unheated greenhouse. Keep it wet, use mineral-free water and give it a cool winter rest.

species.name: Drosera binata
species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Droseraceae - Genus Drosera - Subgenus Phycopsis - Section Phycopsis
species.typeLocality: cape Van Diemen, around Southport, Tas., AU, J.Labillardiere s.n. (G00210238)
species.summary: Elegant forked leaves that unfurl like a green fountain, each tip loaded with sticky glands.
species.description: Drosera binata is a temperate sundew with long, narrow leaves that divide once, twice or many times at the tip, giving it a distinctive forked or antler-like appearance. It grows in wet heath and swamp margins in Australia and New Zealand and dies back to a resting bud in winter. Large specimens can be spectacular in a bog garden or a deep pot.
species.etymology: binata means 'paired' or 'twofold', referring to the forked leaf tips.
species.careGroupTagline: Cold winters, wet summers and full sun.
species.careNotes: Give it full sun and wet feet in summer, then a cool, moist winter dormancy. It can be grown outdoors in a sheltered bog in mild climates.

species.name: Drosera capensis
species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Droseraceae - Genus Drosera - Subgenus Drosera - Section
species.typeLocality: Cape, ZA, Thunberg s.n. (LINN 398.4)
species.summary: The forgiving gateway sundew: long, dewy leaves, pink flowers and a remarkable ability to curl around its prey.
species.description: Drosera capensis is a rosette-forming sundew from the permanently wet Cape lowlands. Its narrow leaves are covered with stalked glands that produce a bead of sticky mucilage; insects that land are trapped, and the leaf slowly rolls inward to bring more glands into contact with the prey. It flowers freely, self-seeds readily and has become one of the most widely cultivated carnivorous plants in the world.
species.etymology: capensis means 'from the Cape', referring to South Africa's Cape region.
species.careGroupTagline: Forgiving, frost-sensitive and happy in a bright window.
species.careNotes: Stand it in rainwater, give it full sun and repot every year or two. It is tolerant of a wide range of conditions but dislikes hard water and dry roots.

species.name: Drosera cistiflora
species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Droseraceae - Genus Drosera - Subgenus Drosera - Section
species.typeLocality: Cape, ZA, Thunberg s.n. (LINN 398.6)
species.summary: A winter-growing Cape sundew with some of the largest and most spectacular flowers in the genus.
species.description: Drosera cistiflora is a winter-growing South African sundew with upright stems and narrow, dewy leaves. Its flowers are unusually large for a sundew and come in shades of pink, purple, white or red. The plant dies back to a rootstock in the dry Cape summer and resumes growth with the winter rains. It is a rewarding but specialised species for growers who can provide a Mediterranean cycle.

species.careNotes: Wet, cool winter growth followed by a dry summer dormancy. Use a deep, very sandy mix and keep the rootstock completely dry but not baked in summer.

species.name: Drosera magnifica
species.typeLocality: Pico do Padre Ângelo, eastern Minas Gerais, Brazil
species.summary: One of the largest sundews in the world, discovered through photographs posted on Facebook and described from a single mountain top in Minas Gerais.
species.description: Drosera magnifica is a giant sundew with a climbing or scrambling stem that can exceed a metre, long dewy leaves and a candelabrum-like inflorescence. It is known from a single mountain top in eastern Minas Gerais, where it grows among sandstone outcrops. The species was described in 2015 after photographs taken by an orchid hunter were recognised as an undescribed sundew, making it one of the first plants discovered through social media.
species.etymology: magnifica means 'magnificent', referring to the plant's striking size and appearance.
species.discoveredBy: Recognised from photographs posted on Facebook by Reginaldo Vasconcelos and described by Fernando Rivadavia and Paulo Gonella.
species.careGroupTagline: Forgiving, frost-sensitive and happy in a bright window.
species.careNotes: Treat as a warm-temperate to subtropical sundew with a very open, sandy mix and strong light. It is large and vigorous in cultivation but has a tiny wild range; propagation material should be traceable and never wild-collected.

species.typeLocality: Wren Creek, on road to Patijan from Peter Lacy's Camp on a tributary of Backsten Creek, W.A., AU, 1. 8. 1996, A.Lowrie 1514 (PERTH 04680502)
species.summary: A striking petiolaris-complex sundew with a hairy stem and a crown of long, dewy leaves.
species.description: Drosera paradoxa comes from the Kimberley region of Western Australia and belongs to the petiolaris complex, a group adapted to a hot, monsoonal climate. It forms an upright, hairy stem topped with a rosette of long leaves. During the dry season it may die back to a hairy resting bud. The contrast between the furry stem and the glistening traps is unforgettable.
species.etymology: paradoxa means 'unexpected' or 'paradoxical', perhaps referring to its unusual appearance for a sundew.

species.summary: A giant, dramatic sundew with long, snaking leaves and a crown of dewy tentacles.
species.description: Drosera regia is one of the largest sundews, forming a rosette of long, narrow leaves that can reach half a metre or more. The leaves are armed with prominent tentacles and the plant has a distinctly regal, almost prehistoric look. It is restricted to a handful of mountain sites in the Western Cape and is considered one of the genus's most threatened species.
species.etymology: regia means 'royal' or 'kingly', a reference to its size and stature.
species.careGroupTagline: Forgiving, frost-sensitive and happy in a bright window.
species.careNotes: Grow it cool and very bright, with a large pot and consistently moist, airy soil. It resents hot roots and stagnant water. This is not the easiest sundew, despite its size.

species.name: Drosera rotundifolia
species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Droseraceae - Genus Drosera - Subgenus Drosera - Section Drosera
species.typeLocality: Europe (LINN 398.2)
species.summary: The classic circumboreal sundew: a tiny rosette of round, red, dew-covered leaves.
species.description: Drosera rotundifolia is one of the most widespread carnivorous plants in the Northern Hemisphere, growing in acid bogs from North America to Europe and Asia. Its round leaves lie flat to the ground and are covered with red tentacles. In summer it sends up a tall scape of small white flowers. It is a lovely plant for a cool bog garden but dislikes warm, stagnant conditions.
species.etymology: rotundifolia means 'round-leaved'.
species.careGroupTagline: Cold winters, wet summers and full sun.
species.careNotes: An outdoor bog plant. Keep it in full sun, in live sphagnum or peat and sand, with cool, clean water. It needs a cold winter dormancy.

species.name: Drosophyllum lusitanicum
species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Drosophyllaceae - Genus Drosophyllum - Subgenus Drosophyllum - Section Drosophyllum
species.summary: A woody, sun-loving Mediterranean carnivore that catches insects on long, dewy leaves.
species.description: Drosophyllum lusitanicum is a shrubby carnivore from the dry south-western corner of Europe and north-western Morocco. Its long, narrow leaves are covered with sticky glands and curl slightly at the tips. Unlike most carnivores, it grows in relatively dry, often alkaline soils. It is famous among growers for being difficult to transplant.
species.etymology: Drosophyllum means 'dew-leaf'; lusitanicum means 'from Lusitania', an old name for Portugal.
species.careGroupTagline: Winter growth, summer drought and brilliant light.
species.careNotes: Deep pot, very free-draining mineral mix, full sun and careful watering. Never disturb the roots; sow in the final container.

species.name: Genlisea violacea
species.classification: Subclass Asteridae - Order Scrophulariales - Family Lentibulariaceae - Genus Genlisea - Subgenus Genlisea - Section Tayloria
species.typeLocality: Serra da Lapa, Serra da Ibitipoca, Minas Gerais, BR, St.Hilaire s.n. (P)
species.summary: A tiny Brazilian corkscrew plant with underground lobster-pot traps and violet flowers.
species.description: Genlisea violacea is a small rosette plant from the wet campos rupestres of Brazil. Its most remarkable feature is underground: spiral, lobster-pot traps that guide tiny invertebrates into a digestive chamber. The plant produces violet flowers on tall scapes. It is a delicate terrarium subject for growers who enjoy the miniature side of carnivory.
species.etymology: violacea means 'violet-coloured', referring to the flowers.
species.careNotes: Wet, bright and warm, with a loose sandy peat mix and live sphagnum on the surface. Keep the mix very wet but aerated.

species.summary: Habropetalum dawei is a sticky leaves (borderline) carnivore from Sierra Leone, described by (Hutch. & Dalz.) Airy Shaw in 1952.
species.description: Habropetalum dawei is a member of the habropetalum genus Habropetalum (family Dioncophyllaceae). Habropetalum dawei is a rare tropical liana in the Dioncophyllaceae. Like its relatives, it has glandular leaves and has been discussed as a possible proto-carnivore. It was described by (Hutch. & Dalz.) Airy Shaw in 1952. The ICPS snapshot records it from Sierra Leone.
species.careNotes: No specialist care group is assigned. Follow the Habropetalum genus care sheet and adjust for the species' native climate.

species.description: Heliamphora chimantensis is endemic to the Chimantá massif in Venezuela. It produces stout, reddish pitchers with a small lid and grows in open, wet, peaty habitats on the tepui summits. Like other Heliamphora, it is a highland plant that depends on cool nights and constant humidity.

species.typeLocality: Mt.Roraima, VE, R.Schomburgk 645 (K000471792)
species.summary: A highland tepui pitcher with nodding white flowers and elegant, red-veined pitchers.
species.description: Heliamphora nutans is the classic sun pitcher from Mount Roraima and neighbouring tepuis in the Guiana Highlands. Its pitchers are formed from rolled leaves with a small, nectar-secreting lid, and the white flowers nod on tall scapes. It grows in wet, peaty, nutrient-poor soil and depends on cool nights and high humidity.
species.etymology: nutans means 'nodding', referring to the flowers.
species.discoveredBy: Collected by Robert Schomburgk on Mount Roraima and described by George Bentham in 1840.
species.careGroupTagline: Cool nights, bright days and cloud-forest humidity.
species.careNotes: Highland conditions: cool nights, high humidity, strong light and constantly moist, airy peat. Warm nights are the main risk.

species.classification: Subclass Asteridae - Order Scrophulariales - Family Martyniaceae - Genus Ibicella - Subgenus Ibicella - Section Ibicella
species.summary: A sticky South American annual with yellow flowers and large, clawed seed pods.
species.description: Ibicella lutea is a sprawling annual from South America, now naturalised in warm regions elsewhere. Its soft, sticky leaves and stems trap small insects, but the plant is only weakly carnivorous. The yellow flowers are followed by large, woody seed pods with curved claws. It is an easy curiosity for a warm, sunny garden.
species.etymology: Ibicella is a diminutive of Ibicella's related genus; lutea means 'yellow'.
species.careNotes: Full sun, poor sandy soil and moderate water. It self-seeds readily in warm climates.

species.description: Martynia annua is a coarse annual from Mexico and Central America, now widespread in the tropics. species.typeLocality: SG, Jack s.n. (SING) Jebb & Cheek
species.summary: A lowland species with squat, flask-shaped pitchers that collect leaf litter and become a miniature ecosystem.
species.description: Nepenthes ampullaria is unusual among pitcher plants because its lower pitchers are squat and flask-shaped, with a small lid that barely covers the opening. In the wild the pitchers collect falling leaves and detritus, and the plant obtains nutrients from the decaying litter and the organisms that live in it. It grows in wet, shaded lowland forest and can form dense carpets.
species.etymology: ampullaria means 'flask-shaped', referring to the pitcher.

species.summary: A recently discovered giant from Palawan, with pitchers large enough to trap rats.
species.description: Nepenthes attenboroughii was discovered on Mount Victoria in Palawan, Philippines, and described in 2009. The pitchers can be among the largest in the genus and are capable of trapping small vertebrates. It grows on ultramafic soil and is highly localised.

species.name: Nepenthes lowii
species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Nepenthaceae - Genus Nepenthes - Subgenus Nepenthes - Section Regiae
species.typeLocality: Kinabalu, MY, Low s.n. (K)
species.summary: A bizarre highland pitcher with a wide, flared mouth and a lid that produces a sugary exudate.
species.description: Nepenthes lowii is a highland species from Borneo with distinctive upper pitchers that are narrow at the base and flare into a wide, almost funnel-like mouth. The lid produces a sweet exudate that attracts tree shrews; the animals feed at the pitcher and defecate into it, providing the plant with nutrients. It is one of the most remarkable examples of plant-animal mutualism in the genus.
species.etymology: Named for Hugh Low, the Victorian plant collector who first discovered many Bornean pitcher plants.
species.discoveredBy: Discovered by Hugh Low and described by Joseph Dalton Hooker in 1859.
species.careGroupTagline: Cool nights, bright days and cloud-forest humidity.
species.careNotes: Highland conditions with a pronounced night drop, high humidity and bright filtered light. It is slow-growing and best for experienced growers.

species.description: Nepenthes maagnawense grows in shrubland at 2300–2700 m on Mt. Maagnaw in the Kitanglad Range. species.name: Nepenthes maximoides
species.typeLocality: Luzon, Philippines, possibly Mt. Banahaw
species.summary: A possibly extinct pitcher plant known from a single herbarium specimen collected more than a century ago.
species.description: Nepenthes maximoides is known from a single historical specimen from Luzon, probably collected on Mt. Banahaw, and had not been recorded for about 110 years when it was described in 2020. Its large, narrowly funnel-shaped upper pitchers and unusual lid appendages resemble those of N. maxima, a striking case of convergent evolution. It is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct).
species.discoveredBy: Recognised in herbarium material by Charles King and Martin Cheek and described in 2020.

species.typeLocality: Mount Saint Paul karst, Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park, Palawan, Philippines, c. 250 m
species.summary: A micro-endemic pitcher plant from vertical limestone walls in Palawan, described in 2025.
species.description: Nepenthes megastoma is known from three locations on vertical limestone walls in the Mount Saint Paul karst formation on Palawan. It has highly branched stems, campanulate pitchers, peltate tendril insertion and dimorphic upper pitchers. The species is assessed as Critically Endangered and appears to be closely related to the Palawan endemic N. philippinensis.

species.name: Nepenthes pongoides
species.fullName: Nepenthes pongoides Damit, Yusof, Jumian & A.S.Rob.
species.typeLocality: Meliau Range, central Sabah, Borneo, Malaysia
species.summary: A recently described giant lowland pitcher plant from an ultramafic peak in Sabah, known from only two subpopulations.
species.description: Nepenthes pongoides is one of the largest Nepenthes described in recent years, with a massive rosette, peltate tendril insertion and a dense, persistent covering of long reddish hairs. It is known from the low-elevation Meliau Range in central Sabah, where only a few dozen mature individuals have been observed. The species was formally described in 2024 and assessed as Critically Endangered.
species.etymology: The epithet refers to the orangutan (Pongo), reflecting the plant's reddish, hairy appearance.
species.discoveredBy: Described by Alviana Damit, S. Yusof, J. Jumian and Alastair S. Robinson in 2024.
species.careGroupTagline: Warm nights, high humidity and steady heat.
species.careNotes: A warm lowland species. Provide steady warmth, high humidity, bright filtered light and an open epiphytic mix. It is not yet widely established in cultivation.
species.conservationNote: Known from two subpopulations and assessed as Critically Endangered. Habitat protection is the priority; horticultural material is extremely limited.

species.name: Nepenthes rajah
species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Nepenthaceae - Genus Nepenthes - Subgenus Nepenthes - Section Villosae
species.typeLocality: Kinabalu, MY, Low s.n. (K)
species.summary: The giant of the pitcher plants: enormous, blood-red pitchers that can hold litres of fluid.
species.description: Nepenthes rajah is a highland species from the slopes of Mount Kinabalu and neighbouring mountains in Sabah, Borneo. It produces some of the largest pitchers in the genus, capable of holding several litres of digestive fluid. The pitchers are often reddish and have a massive, ribbed peristome. The species is slow-growing, long-lived and highly prized by collectors, but it is also one of the most threatened.
species.etymology: rajah means 'king' or 'prince' in Malay, a reference to the extraordinary size of the pitchers.
species.discoveredBy: Discovered by Hugh Low in 1851 and described by Joseph Dalton Hooker in 1859.
species.careGroupTagline: Cool nights, bright days and cloud-forest humidity.
species.careNotes: Cool nights, high humidity, bright filtered light and a large, airy pot. It is slow and expensive to grow; buy only legal, nursery-propagated plants.

photo.alt: Photograph of Nepenthes rajah

species.conservationNote: Endemic to a small area of Sabah and threatened by habitat disturbance and collection. Protected under CITES.

species.summary: A Bornean highlander famous for its broad, flared peristome and striking striped pitchers.
species.description: Nepenthes veitchii is a variable species from Borneo, often growing as an epiphyte on mossy trees. Its pitchers have an exceptionally wide, flared peristome, sometimes striped in red and yellow. Lower and upper pitchers can look quite different. It is a highland to intermediate species and a favourite among collectors for its sculptural peristome.
species.etymology: Named for the Veitch nursery family, who sponsored many Victorian plant collectors.
species.careGroupTagline: Cool nights, bright days and cloud-forest humidity.

species.summary: One of the largest butterworts, with broad, pale green leaves that can span a dinner plate.
species.description: Pinguicula gigantea is a Mexican butterwort and one of the largest species in the genus. Its rosettes of broad, fleshy leaves are covered with sticky glands and can become very large in cultivation. In winter it forms a smaller, succulent rosette. It is a rewarding plant for a bright windowsill or terrarium.
species.etymology: gigantea means 'giant', referring to the size of the rosette.
species.careGroupTagline: Summer carnivory, winter succulence.
species.careNotes: Wet and actively growing in summer; much drier in winter when the succulent rosette forms. Use a mineral-rich, well-drained mix.

species.typeLocality: Dauphine, FR, Lamarck s.n. (?P)
species.summary: A European bog butterwort with handsome violet flowers and a cold winter hibernaculum.
species.description: Pinguicula grandiflora is a temperate butterwort from wet, calcareous habitats in western Europe. It forms a rosette of pale green, sticky leaves and produces large, violet flowers in spring. In winter it dies back to a tight hibernaculum. It is a good choice for a cool bog garden or an unheated greenhouse.
species.etymology: grandiflora means 'large-flowered'.
species.careGroupTagline: Cold winters, wet summers and full sun.
species.careNotes: Keep it wet and cool, with bright light and a cold winter dormancy. It dislikes warm, stagnant conditions.

species.classification: Subclass Asteridae - Order Scrophulariales - Family Martyniaceae - Genus Proboscidea - Subgenus Proboscidea - Section Proboscidea
species.summary: A sticky summer annual with mauve flowers and dramatic, hooked seed pods.
species.description: Proboscidea louisianica is a fast-growing annual from the south-central USA and Mexico. Its large, sticky leaves trap small insects, and its flowers are followed by woody seed pods with long, curved claws that inspired the common name. It is an easy and unusual summer annual for a sunny garden.
species.etymology: Proboscidea means 'like a proboscis', referring to the long, curved seed pods; louisianica refers to Louisiana.
species.careNotes: Full sun, moderate water and poor, well-drained soil. Sow after the last frost and let the pods dry on the plant.

species.description: Roridula dentata is a member of the dewsticks genus Roridula (family Roridulaceae). Roridula is a South African shrub with long, sticky leaves that trap insects. Unusually, the plant does not digest its prey directly: a resident bug (Pameridea) feeds on the trapped insects and the plant absorbs nutrients from the bug's droppings. It was described by L. in 1764. The ICPS snapshot records it from South Africa. The type locality is Cape, ZA, (LINN 284.1).

species.classification: Subclass Ericidae - Order Ericales (incl. Sarraceniales) - Family Roridulaceae - Genus Roridula - Subgenus Roridula - Section Roridula
species.typeLocality: Caledon, Riviersonderend Mountains, Cape, ZA, Ecklon & Zeyher (CGE)
species.summary: A sticky South African shrub that outsources digestion to resident assassin bugs.
species.description: Roridula gorgonias is a woody shrub from the Cape fynbos with long, narrow leaves covered in sticky glands. It traps insects, but instead of digesting them directly it relies on resident Pameridea bugs that feed on the catch; the plant absorbs nutrients from the bugs' droppings. This indirect carnivory is a remarkable example of mutualism.
species.etymology: Roridula means 'slightly dewy'; gorgonias may refer to the Gorgons, perhaps because of the plant's striking, snaky appearance.

species.synonym: =Sarracenia purpurea var. burkii Schnell * Sarracenia flava L.

species.description: Sarracenia 'Abandoned Hope' is an ICPS-registered cultivar of Sarracenia purpurea var. burkii Schnell. Its registered parentage is Sarracenia purpurea var. burkii Schnell × Sarracenia flava. The cultivar authority is D'Amato. It was originated by P.D'Amato, California Carnivores, Forestville, USA, 1989. The registration was submitted by P.D'Amato on 15 January 2000. It was published in Carniv.Pl.Newslett.29:46 (2000). The registered etymology is: from the sign at the entrance to hell in Dante's Inferno: Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here. Its registration standard is Carniv.Pl.Newslett.29:48 (2000). Cultivar characteristics are defined by that registration; consult the ICPS register entry for the full description.

The registered etymology is: alluding to association with royalty due to a strong feeling (of the nominants) of elegance and delicate ruffles. Its registration standard is Carniv.Pl.Newslett.27:33 (cover) (1998) (only pitchers with areolae in the foreground; the pitchers in the background do not belong to this cultivar). species.summary: Tall, elegant yellow-green trumpets with a nectar-rich rim that attracts a steady stream of insects.
species.description: Sarracenia flava is one of the tallest North American pitcher plants, forming bold, yellow-green trumpets that can reach a metre in good conditions. The hood is upright and the rim secretes nectar that lures insects into the pitcher. In spring the plant produces large, nodding yellow flowers. It is a striking and relatively easy species for a sunny bog.
species.etymology: flava means 'yellow', referring to the flowers and often the pitchers.

species.careNotes: Full sun, wet feet and a cold winter dormancy. Give it plenty of space; it is a tall grower.

It grows in wet pine savannas in the south-eastern USA and is vulnerable to habitat loss.

species.summary: A neat, hooded pitcher with translucent windows that confuse trapped insects.
species.description: Sarracenia minor produces slender, hooded pitchers with white patches near the top. Sunlight passes through these translucent windows, confusing insects inside the pitcher and encouraging them to tire and fall into the digestive fluid. It is native to the coastal plain of the south-eastern USA and is a charming, manageable species for a bog garden.
species.etymology: minor means 'smaller', distinguishing it from its larger relatives.

species.summary: A low, decumbent pitcher that works like a lobster pot, with a hooded opening and inward-pointing hairs.
species.description: Sarracenia psittacina is unlike the tall trumpet pitchers: its pitchers lie flat or arch close to the ground, with a hooded opening that resembles a parrot's beak. Insects enter through the hood and are guided inward by downward-pointing hairs, unable to find their way out. It grows in wet pine savannas and bogs in the south-eastern USA.
species.etymology: psittacina means 'parrot-like', referring to the shape of the pitcher opening.
species.careGroupTagline: Cold winters, wet summers and full sun.
species.careNotes: Keep it wet and in full sun, with a cold winter dormancy. It appreciates a shallow water level and can be grown at the edge of a bog.

species.summary: The squat, purple-veined pitcher of cold bogs, hardy enough for an outdoor bog garden.
species.description: Sarracenia purpurea is the most widespread North American pitcher plant and the floral emblem of Newfoundland and Labrador. Its pitchers are short, squat and often heavily veined with purple, with a hood that keeps out rain. It grows in cold, acidic bogs and is one of the hardiest carnivorous plants, making it a favourite for outdoor bog gardens.
species.etymology: purpurea means 'purple', referring to the colour of the pitchers and flowers.

species.classification: Subclass Caryophyllidae - Order Nepenthales - Family Dioncophyllaceae - Genus Triphyophyllum - Subgenus Triphyophyllum - Section Triphyophyllum
species.summary: A West African liana that becomes carnivorous only during part of its life cycle.
species.description: Triphyophyllum peltatum is a tropical liana and one of the few known facultative carnivores. Juvenile plants produce sticky, glandular leaves that trap insects; as the plant matures it switches to ordinary leaves and a climbing habit. It is a fascinating botanical curiosity and is not cultivated as a houseplant.
species.etymology: Triphyophyllum means 'three-leaf-types', referring to its three distinct leaf forms; peltatum means 'shield-shaped'.
species.careNotes: Not recommended for cultivation. It needs tropical rainforest conditions and a large climbing structure.

species.name: Utricularia 'Yog-Sothoth'
species.description: Utricularia 'Yog-Sothoth' is an ICPS-registered cultivar of Utricularia calycifida. The cultivar authority is B.Rice. It was originated by ?, from VE, before 1990. The registration was submitted by B.Rice, Davis, USA on 22 October 1999. It was published in Carniv.Pl.Newslett.29:17 (2000). The registered etymology is: notes the potent and enigmatic entity mentioned in various stories by H.P. Lovecraft, the original Yog-Sothoth and the cultivar share features such as peculiar venation, countless sucking mouths, and an insatiable appetite. Its registration standard is Carniv.Pl.Newslett.21:10 & 12 (1992). Cultivar characteristics are defined by that registration; consult the ICPS register entry for the full description.

species.summary: A cheerful terrestrial bladderwort with tiny violet flowers that look like rabbits' faces.
species.description: Utricularia sandersonii is a small terrestrial bladderwort from South Africa. It spreads into a bright green carpet of leaves and produces pale violet flowers with a distinctive rabbit-like shape. The actual traps are tiny bladders hidden in the soil. It is one of the easiest bladderworts and a favourite for terrariums and windowsills.
species.etymology: Named after John Sanderson, a 19th-century plant collector in South Africa.

species.summary: A free-floating aquatic bladderwort that fills summer ponds with yellow flowers and invisible traps.
species.description: Utricularia vulgaris is a widespread aquatic bladderwort of Eurasia. It floats just below the surface, producing finely divided leaves and small bladder traps that capture tiny aquatic invertebrates. In summer it sends up yellow flowers above the water. It is a beautiful pond plant but can spread aggressively in rich water.
