cultivarSource.note: Names and registration facts from the ICPS Carnivorous Plant Names Resource registered-cultivar list. Summaries are original editorial text; the ICPS register remains the authority for the full description.

genera.nativeRange: Scattered freshwater wetlands across Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia
genera.description: Aldrovanda vesiculosa is a rootless, free-floating aquatic sundew whose whorls of leaves look like the paddles of a waterwheel. Each leaf ends in a small snap trap, one of the fastest active traps in the plant kingdom. The plant spends summer at the water surface and survives winter as a dormant turion at the bottom of the pond.
genera.identification: Look for floating whorls of six to eight leaves, each tipped with a translucent, hinged trap and fine trigger hairs. The traps are only a few millimetres long.
genera.ecology: It grows in shallow, acidic, nutrient-poor water and is sensitive to pollution, drainage and eutrophication. Wild populations are widely scattered and declining, making it a flagship for wetland conservation.

care.overview: A specialist aquarium and pond plant. It needs soft, acidic water, strong light and a cool winter rest. It is not a beginner plant.
care.light: Full sun to very bright light; outdoors in a shallow tub is best.
care.water: Soft, acidic, mineral-free water. Keep the water warm in summer and cool in winter; avoid hard tap water entirely.
care.soil: No soil. Float the plants in water; add a little live sphagnum or a mesh anchor if needed.
care.temperature: Summer 20–30°C; winter 4–10°C for turion formation and dormancy.
care.dormancy: Forms turions in autumn. Keep turions cool and submerged; restart in spring.
care.feeding: Feed tiny aquatic invertebrates or a very dilute aquarium invertebrate food. Do not overfeed.
care.propagation: Division of floating stems in summer; turions in winter.
care.problems: Hard water, algae, overheating, snails and fish. Wild-collected plants are best avoided.

genera.nativeRange: Australia and New Guinea, with the greatest diversity in the tropical north and south-west
genera.description: Byblis leaves are covered with glandular hairs that glitter in the sun and produce a rainbow-like sheen. Insects stick to the mucilage and are digested by the plant. The genus includes small annuals and taller, shrubby perennials, and is unrelated to the superficially similar sundews.
genera.identification: Leaves are narrow and grass-like, with sticky glands on the upper surface and a simple or branched stem. Flowers are usually mauve to purple.
genera.ecology: Most species grow in sandy, seasonally wet heathland. Annuals complete their life cycle in the wet season and survive the dry season as seed; perennials develop woody stems and may die back to a rootstock.

care.overview: Bright light, warm temperatures and constantly damp, sandy, nutrient-poor soil. Annuals are best raised from seed each season.
care.light: Full sun to very bright light.
care.water: Stand in 1–3 cm of mineral-free water during growth. Never let the mix dry out while plants are growing.
care.soil: Peat : sand 1:1, or a very sandy peat mix. Keep it open and low in nutrients.
care.dormancy: Annuals die after seeding; perennials may die back in the dry season.
care.feeding: They catch their own insects. Do not fertilise.
care.propagation: Seed, sown on the surface of wet sandy peat. Perennials can be divided.
care.problems: Damping-off, root disturbance, hard water and aphids.

annual.label: Annual
annual.notes: Sow fresh seed in warm, bright conditions and keep the surface wet. Plants self-seed readily when happy.

perennial.label: Perennial
perennial.notes: Grow in deep pots so the rootstock has room. Reduce water during the dry-season rest.

genera.nativeRange: A small corner of the south-west Western Australian coast near Albany
genera.description: Cephalotus follicularis is the only species in its family and one of the most distinctive pitcher plants. It produces a basal rosette of ordinary leaves and ribbed, tooth-rimmed pitchers with a lid. The pitchers are small but remarkably efficient, and the plant's strange, almost reptilian look has made it a collector's favourite.
genera.identification: Squat pitchers with a toothed peristome and a domed lid; mature plants form tight clumps. The pitcher body is often mottled green, red and purple.
genera.ecology: It grows in sandy, peaty swamps and seepages in a Mediterranean climate, with wet winters and drier summers. Habitat loss and illegal collection are significant threats.

care.overview: A compact, slow-growing plant for a cool, bright position. It resents hot roots, hard water and being kept bone dry.
care.light: Bright light with some direct sun; avoid scorching summer heat.
care.water: Tray water with mineral-free water. Keep the mix moist year-round, slightly drier in summer.
care.soil: Peat : sand : perlite 2:1:1. A top dressing of live sphagnum helps keep humidity even.
care.temperature: Cool to intermediate: 10–25°C. Protect from prolonged heat above 30°C.
care.dormancy: No true dormancy. Growth slows in hot, dry summers; do not let the roots desiccate.
care.feeding: Feed only occasionally with small insects; the pitchers catch their own food outdoors.
care.propagation: Leaf cuttings, division, root cuttings and seed. Be patient: seedlings are slow.
care.problems: Root rot from stale, waterlogged soil, hard water, mealybugs and scale.

genera.nativeRange: South America, mainly Brazil and neighbouring countries
genera.description: Craniolaria is a small genus of sticky-leaved annuals in the Martyniaceae. The leaves and stems are covered with glandular hairs that trap small insects, but the plants are not as strongly carnivorous as Drosera or Pinguicula. They are grown mostly as curiosities and for their unusual seed pods.
genera.identification: Soft, hairy annual with opposite leaves and tubular flowers; the fruit develops a long, woody beak.
genera.ecology: Seasonally dry, open habitats. The sticky glands are thought to deter herbivores as well as capture small insects.

care.overview: An easy warm-season annual from seed. Treat it as a drought-tolerant curiosity rather than a high-maintenance carnivore.
care.water: Moderate; let the surface dry between waterings. Avoid waterlogging.
care.soil: Free-draining sandy loam or a cactus-style mix.
care.temperature: Warm; sow after the last frost.
care.dormancy: Annual; dies after setting seed.
care.feeding: No feeding required.
care.propagation: Seed sown directly in warm conditions.
care.problems: Aphids, spider mites and damping-off in cool, wet soil.

genera.nativeRange: Mountain seeps and serpentine wetlands of northern California and south-western Oregon
genera.description: Darlingtonia californica is instantly recognisable: its tubular leaves arch over into a hooded head with a forked appendage that looks like a snake's tongue. Insects enter through openings under the hood and are guided down into the pitcher. The plant is the only species in its genus and is prized by collectors for its sculptural form.
genera.identification: Hooded, cobra-like pitchers with a forked 'tongue' and a small opening beneath the hood. Pitchers arise from a creeping rhizome.
genera.ecology: It grows in cold, flowing seeps and fens, often on serpentine soil. It needs cool roots and clean water; wild populations are threatened by water extraction, development and poaching.

care.overview: The key is cool, moving water and cool roots. This is not a plant for a hot windowsill.
care.light: Full sun to bright light; in hot climates provide afternoon shade.
care.water: Constant flow of cool, mineral-free water is ideal. Keep the mix wet and the roots below 25°C.
care.soil: Peat : perlite : sand 2:1:1, with a top dressing of live sphagnum.
care.dormancy: Winter dormancy is required. Keep cool and moist, not frozen solid.
care.feeding: Outdoor plants catch their own insects. Do not fertilise.
care.propagation: Division of rhizomes in late winter; seed (slow and variable).
care.problems: Root rot in stagnant water, heat stress, aphids and scale.

genera.nativeRange: A small area of coastal North and South Carolina, USA
genera.description: Dionaea muscipula is the most famous carnivorous plant in the world. Each leaf ends in two hinged lobes armed with trigger hairs and marginal teeth; two touches within about twenty seconds can snap the trap shut. The genus is monotypic, but centuries of cultivation have produced an extraordinary range of cultivars.
genera.identification: Paired, jaw-like lobes with marginal teeth and three trigger hairs on each lobe. Traps are held on short, broad petioles in a rosette.
genera.ecology: It grows in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor pine savannas and bogs that depend on frequent fire. Wild populations are threatened by habitat loss and poaching; the species is protected in the wild.

care.overview: A rewarding beginner plant if it gets full sun, clean water and a cool winter dormancy. The most common mistake is keeping it warm and wet indoors all winter.
care.light: Full sun outdoors; a very bright, sunny windowsill indoors.
care.water: Stand in 2–5 cm of mineral-free water during growth. Use rainwater, distilled or reverse-osmosis water.
care.soil: Peat : perlite or silica sand 1:1. Never use ordinary potting soil or fertiliser.
care.dormancy: Needs a cool winter rest of 8–12 weeks. Reduce water but do not let the mix dry completely.
care.feeding: Feed live insects occasionally, or let the plant catch its own. Never feed meat or fertiliser.
care.propagation: Division in late winter, leaf cuttings, flower-stalk cuttings and seed.
care.problems: Root rot, sunburn after a sudden move, aphids, spider mites and scale.

genera.nativeRange: Tropical West and Central Africa
genera.description: Dioncophyllum thollonii is a tropical liana in the Dioncophyllaceae, a family that also contains the famous Triphyophyllum. Its leaves bear glandular structures and the plant has been discussed as a possible proto-carnivore, but it is not a practical cultivated carnivore. It is included here for completeness of the ICPS register.
genera.identification: A woody liana with alternate leaves and hooked climbing structures; the glandular leaf surfaces are subtle.
genera.ecology: Rainforest liana of tropical Africa. Its carnivorous status is debated and difficult to study in the field.

care.overview: Not recommended for cultivation. It requires tropical rainforest conditions and a large climbing structure, and is essentially a botanical-garden curiosity.
care.water: High humidity and evenly moist, free-draining soil.
care.soil: Loose, humus-rich tropical mix.
care.dormancy: None.
care.feeding: Not applicable in cultivation.
care.propagation: Seed or stem cuttings, with difficulty.
care.problems: Not a houseplant; leave wild plants undisturbed.

genera.nativeRange: Every continent except Antarctica, with centres of diversity in Australia, South Africa and South America
genera.description: Drosera is the largest genus of carnivorous plants, with more than 190 accepted species. Each leaf is covered with stalked glands that secrete a glistening drop of mucilage; insects stick, and the leaf may slowly curl around the prey. Sundews range from tiny pygmy rosettes to the giant Drosera regia, and from tropical epiphytes to winter-growing tuberous species.
genera.identification: Leaves with visible stalked glands and clear mucilage droplets. Growth forms include rosettes, upright stems, climbing stems, tubers and pygmy rosettes.
genera.ecology: Sundews occupy nutrient-poor wetlands, seepages, heathlands and inselbergs. Many are fire-adapted, and several groups have precise seasonal dormancy. Some species are among the most threatened plants in their habitats.

care.overview: Sundews want bright light, mineral-free water and a nutrient-poor acidic mix. The right care depends strongly on the species group: temperate, subtropical, Cape winter-growing, pygmy, tuberous, petiolaris or annual.
care.light: Full sun to very bright light. Indoors, use a powerful grow light.
care.water: Tray water with rainwater, distilled or reverse-osmosis water. Keep the mix wet during growth.
care.soil: Peat : perlite or silica sand 1:1. Some groups prefer sandier or more organic mixes.
care.temperature: Depends on the group. Temperate species need cool winters; tropical species need warmth year-round.
care.dormancy: Many species have a dry, cool or cold dormant season. Match the group.
care.feeding: Let them catch their own insects. A very occasional tiny insect is enough; never fertilise the soil.
care.propagation: Seed, leaf cuttings, root cuttings and division, depending on the group.
care.problems: Hard water, root rot, aphids, thrips, spider mites, mildew and drying out.

temperate.label: Temperate
temperate.water: Stand in 2–5 cm of mineral-free water during growth.
temperate.temperature: Cool to mild; winter cold is required.
temperate.dormancy: Cold winter dormancy. Many die back to resting buds.
temperate.notes: Hardy outdoor bog plants for temperate climates. Keep the bog wet and open to the sun.

subtropical.label: Subtropical / warm-temperate
subtropical.temperature: Warm to mild; protect from hard frost.
subtropical.dormancy: Growth slows in winter; no hard dormancy.
subtropical.notes: The forgiving group that includes Drosera capensis and D. aliciae. Good beginner sundews.

cape.label: Cape winter-growing
cape.water: Wet during winter growth; much drier in summer dormancy.
cape.temperature: Cool, Mediterranean; protect from summer heat.
cape.notes: These South African species grow in winter rain and rest dry in summer. Do not keep them wet year-round.

pygmy.label: Pygmy sundew
pygmy.light: Full sun; strong light keeps the rosettes compact and colourful.
pygmy.water: Wet during winter growth; drier in summer.
pygmy.soil: Very sandy peat, low in nutrients.
pygmy.temperature: Cool to mild; avoid hot, humid nights.
pygmy.dormancy: Dry summer dormancy; many form gemmae.
pygmy.notes: Pygmy sundews are small, jewel-like Australian species. Gemmae are the easiest way to propagate them.

tuberous.label: Tuberous
tuberous.water: Wet during winter growth; completely dry during summer dormancy.
tuberous.soil: Deep, very sandy peat with sharp drainage.
tuberous.notes: Use deep pots so the tuber has room. Keep dry in summer and resume watering when new growth appears.

petiolaris.label: Petiolaris complex
petiolaris.water: Wet during the wet season; drier during the dry-season dormancy.
petiolaris.dormancy: Dry-season dormancy; plants may die back to a hairy resting bud.
petiolaris.notes: A challenging group from tropical northern Australia. They need heat, light and a pronounced dry rest.

annual.label: Annual
annual.notes: Sow fresh seed and let the colony self-seed. A fast, fun group.

genera.nativeRange: South-western Iberia and north-western Morocco
genera.description: Drosophyllum lusitanicum is a shrubby, woody-based carnivore from the dry Mediterranean fringe. Its long, narrow leaves are covered with sticky glands and curl slightly at the tips. Unlike most carnivores it grows in relatively dry, alkaline or neutral soils, and it is notoriously difficult to transplant.
genera.identification: A woody shrub with long, narrow, dewy leaves and yellow flowers. The leaves are not arranged in a rosette and the plant can reach 1 m across.
genera.ecology: It grows in open, dry, sunny scrub on sandy or stony soils, often after fire. It is threatened by development, afforestation and collection.

care.overview: Grow it in a deep, well-drained pot, keep the roots dry-ish, and never disturb the roots. This is a plant for experienced growers.
care.water: Water deeply but infrequently, then let the mix dry. Avoid tray water and humid, stagnant air.
care.soil: A very free-draining mineral mix: coarse sand, perlite, pumice and a little peat or leaf mould.
care.temperature: Mediterranean: warm, dry summers and cool, damp winters. Protect from frost.
care.dormancy: No true dormancy, but growth slows in the hottest part of summer.
care.feeding: Self-catches; do not feed.
care.propagation: Seed, sown in deep pots. Avoid transplanting; sow in the final container.
care.problems: Root disturbance, rot, spider mites and scale.

genera.nativeRange: Tropical Africa, Madagascar and South America, with a centre of diversity in Brazil
genera.description: Genlisea is a genus of small rosette plants related to Utricularia. Below ground it produces remarkable spiral, lobster-pot traps that guide tiny invertebrates into a digestive chamber. The traps are among the most complex in the plant kingdom. Many species have yellow or violet flowers on tall scapes.
genera.identification: Small rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves with tall flower scapes. The real traps are underground and rarely seen; repotting reveals the corkscrew structures.
genera.ecology: They grow in wet, sandy, nutrient-poor soils and seepages, often in seasonal savanna or campos rupestres. Some species are aquatic or semi-aquatic.

care.overview: Treat Genlisea like a small terrestrial Utricularia: wet, bright and nutrient-poor. The underground traps need a loose, airy mix.
care.water: Keep the mix very wet; tray water is fine.
care.soil: Peat : sand : perlite 1:1:1, with live sphagnum on the surface.
care.temperature: Warm to intermediate; protect from frost.
care.dormancy: Some species die back to a resting bud in the dry season.
care.feeding: Do not feed; the traps capture microfauna.
care.propagation: Leaf cuttings, division, seed.
care.problems: Algae, aphids, drying out, root rot in stale water.

genera.nativeRange: Tropical West Africa
genera.description: Habropetalum dawei is a rare tropical liana in the Dioncophyllaceae. Like its relatives, it has glandular leaves and has been discussed as a possible proto-carnivore. It is not cultivated as a carnivorous plant and is included primarily for completeness of the ICPS register.
genera.identification: Woody liana with alternate leaves and hooked climbing structures; flowers are large and showy.
genera.ecology: Tropical forest liana, poorly known. Its carnivorous status is uncertain.

care.overview: Not recommended for cultivation; it needs tropical forest conditions and a large climbing structure.
care.water: High humidity and evenly moist, free-draining soil.
care.soil: Humus-rich tropical mix.
care.dormancy: None.
care.feeding: Not applicable.
care.propagation: Seed or cuttings, with difficulty.
care.problems: Not a houseplant; leave wild plants undisturbed.

genera.nativeRange: Tepuis of the Guiana Highlands in Venezuela, Guyana and Brazil
genera.description: Heliamphora species grow on the remote, rain-lashed summits of the Guiana Highlands. Their pitchers are formed from rolled leaves with a small, often red-veined lid and a nectar-secreting rim. They are among the most distinctive pitcher plants and can form dense, sculptural clumps.
genera.identification: Tall, slender or squat pitchers with a small lid, often red-veined, emerging from a rhizome. Flowers are white to pink on tall scapes.
genera.ecology: They grow in wet, peaty, nutrient-poor soils on tepui summits and slopes, often in full sun and constant wind. Endemism is high and many species have tiny ranges.

care.overview: A highland plant: strong light, high humidity, cool nights and constantly moist, airy soil. Warm nights are the main killer.
care.light: Very bright light; full sun is often tolerated if humidity is high.
care.water: Mineral-free water, kept cool. Top-water frequently and keep the mix wet.
care.soil: Peat : perlite : live sphagnum 1:1:1, in a tall pot.
care.temperature: Day 18–26°C; night 8–16°C. A night drop is essential.
care.dormancy: No true dormancy, though growth slows in winter.
care.feeding: Small insects in the pitchers; do not fertilise.
care.propagation: Division of rhizomes, seed.
care.problems: Heat stress, root rot, hard water, aphids and scale.

genera.nativeRange: South America, naturalised in warm regions elsewhere
genera.description: Ibicella lutea is a sprawling annual with soft, sticky, strongly scented leaves and yellow flowers. It traps small insects on glandular hairs but is only weakly carnivorous. The common name comes from the large, woody, claw-like seed pods.
genera.identification: Large, opposite, sticky leaves; yellow tubular flowers; distinctive hooked seed capsules.
genera.ecology: A weed of disturbed, warm, often dry ground. It is fast-growing and self-seeds readily.

care.overview: An easy annual curiosity. Grow it in full sun and poor, well-drained soil; do not baby it.
care.water: Moderate; let the surface dry between waterings.
care.soil: Poor, sandy or stony soil with sharp drainage.
care.dormancy: Annual; dies after seeding.
care.feeding: No feeding needed.
care.propagation: Seed. Soak the hard seed coat first.
care.problems: Aphids, spider mites, powdery mildew.

genera.nativeRange: Mexico and Central America; naturalised in the tropics
genera.description: Martynia annua is a sticky, glandular annual in the Martyniaceae. It catches small insects on its leaves and stems but is not a true carnivore in the strict sense. The plant is grown mainly for its dramatic, hooked seed pods.
genera.identification: Coarse annual with opposite, sticky-hairy leaves, pinkish tubular flowers and large wooden seed pods with two curved claws.
genera.ecology: Disturbed ground, roadsides and dry scrub in the tropics and subtropics.

care.overview: Easy from seed in warm, sunny conditions. Treat it as a curiosity annual.
care.water: Moderate; well-drained soil.
care.soil: Poor, sandy loam.
care.dormancy: Annual.
care.feeding: No feeding.
care.propagation: Seed.
care.problems: Aphids and spider mites.

genera.nativeRange: Old World tropics: South-East Asia, Madagascar, Seychelles, New Guinea, northern Australia and islands of the Indian and Pacific Oceans
genera.description: Nepenthes is the great genus of tropical pitcher plants, with more than 120 accepted species and a bewildering array of natural hybrids. The pitchers are modified leaf tips, often brightly coloured, with a slippery peristome and a lid. They range from tiny ground pitchers to the enormous, rat-dissolving pitchers of Nepenthes rajah.
genera.identification: Pitchers with a distinct peristome and lid, usually produced at the end of a tendril. Lower and upper pitchers often look completely different.
genera.ecology: They grow from sea-level swamps to cloud-forest summits, on ultramafic soils, sandstone cliffs and epiphytically in mossy forest. Many have tiny ranges and are threatened by habitat loss and collection.

care.overview: Nepenthes care depends on altitude. Lowland species want warmth and humidity; highland species want a cool night drop. Intermediate forms are the most forgiving.
care.light: Bright, filtered light. Avoid harsh midday sun on young plants.
care.water: Keep the mix evenly moist but airy. Use mineral-free water; never let the pot sit in stagnant water.
care.soil: Sphagnum moss, perlite and bark, or a loose peat : perlite : bark mix.
care.temperature: Depends on the group; see the specific care group.
care.dormancy: No dormancy. Growth slows in cool or very dry conditions.
care.feeding: Feed small insects into the pitchers or use a very dilute orchid fertiliser occasionally. Do not overfeed.
care.propagation: Stem cuttings, basal shoots, tissue culture and seed.
care.problems: Root rot, crown rot, thrips, mealybugs, scale, sudden humidity drops.

lowland.label: Lowland
lowland.notes: Warm, humid and steady. Good for beginners in tropical climates; challenging in cool houses.

highland.label: Highland
highland.notes: The night drop is essential. Use a cool greenhouse, cellar or terrarium with night cooling.

intermediate.label: Intermediate
intermediate.notes: The most adaptable group. Many popular hybrids thrive here.

genera.nativeRange: Northern Hemisphere, with centres of diversity in Mexico and the Mediterranean; also tropical Americas
genera.description: Pinguicula leaves are flat, usually pale green rosettes covered with microscopic sticky glands. Small insects stick to the leaf and are digested in a shallow depression. The genus includes temperate bog species, tropical epiphytes and the remarkable Mexican 'butterworts' that form succulent winter rosettes.
genera.identification: Flat, fleshy rosettes with a greasy, glandular surface. Flowers are usually violet, pink, white or yellow on tall scapes.
genera.ecology: They grow in wet, nutrient-poor habitats: bogs, seeps, limestone cliffs and tropical cloud forest. Mexican species often grow on vertical rocks and have a pronounced dry season.

care.overview: Pinguicula care splits into three broad groups: Mexican, temperate and tropical. Getting the dormancy right is the key.
care.light: Bright light; Mexican species tolerate more sun than temperate ones.
care.water: Tray water with mineral-free water during growth; reduce or stop during dormancy.
care.soil: Peat : perlite : sand, or a mineral mix for Mexican species.
care.dormancy: Mexican species form succulent winter rosettes; temperate species die back to hibernacula; tropical species have no dormancy.
care.feeding: Self-catches small insects. Do not feed large prey or fertilise.
care.propagation: Leaf cuttings, division, seed.
care.problems: Rot, hard water, aphids, thrips, mealybugs.

mexican.label: Mexican
mexican.water: Wet during summer growth; almost dry during the winter succulent rosette.
mexican.soil: Equal parts peat, perlite and vermiculite, with a little sand; slightly alkaline is often used.
mexican.temperature: Warm days, cool nights; protect from frost.
mexican.dormancy: Dry winter dormancy with a small, succulent rosette.
mexican.notes: The classic Mexican butterworts. Keep dry in winter and resume watering when carnivorous leaves appear.

temperate.label: Temperate
temperate.water: Wet during growth; moist but not waterlogged in winter.
temperate.temperature: Cool to mild; winter cold required.
temperate.notes: Hardy bog butterworts for cool climates. They die back to a tight winter bud.

tropical.label: Tropical
tropical.notes: Warm, humid species from the Neotropics. Protect from cold and keep the air moving.

genera.nativeRange: North and South America, mainly Mexico and the south-western USA
genera.description: Proboscidea species are sticky-leaved annuals or short-lived perennials, famous for their woody seed pods with long, curved claws. The glandular leaves trap small insects but the plants are only weakly carnivorous. They are easy, fast-growing summer annuals.
genera.identification: Large, sticky, opposite leaves; tubular pink or purple flowers; long, hooked seed pods.
genera.ecology: Warm, dry, disturbed ground and desert washes. The claws help the seed pods attach to passing animals.

care.overview: An easy, fast annual for a warm sunny spot. Grow it for its strange seed pods as much as for its sticky leaves.
care.water: Moderate; drought-tolerant once established.
care.soil: Poor, sandy, free-draining soil.
care.dormancy: Annual.
care.feeding: No feeding.
care.propagation: Seed; soak and nick the hard coat.
care.problems: Aphids, spider mites, powdery mildew.

genera.nativeRange: Fynbos of the south-western Cape, South Africa
genera.description: Roridula is a South African shrub with long, sticky leaves that trap insects. Unusually, the plant does not digest its prey directly: a resident bug (Pameridea) feeds on the trapped insects and the plant absorbs nutrients from the bug's droppings. This delicate mutualism makes Roridula one of the most fascinating plants in the Cape flora.
genera.identification: A woody shrub with narrow, sticky leaves and small pink or white flowers. Look for the resident assassin bugs on the leaves.
genera.ecology: It grows in nutrient-poor fynbos on sandy soils. The plant depends on its resident bugs; plants without them can be nutrient-starved.

care.overview: A specialist Mediterranean shrub. It needs sandy, acidic soil, full sun, good airflow and its pollinating/resident insects for long-term health.
care.water: Keep moist during winter growth; reduce in summer but do not bake the roots.
care.soil: Very sandy, acidic peat mix with sharp drainage.
care.dormancy: Growth slows in the dry summer.
care.feeding: Do not feed the plant; it relies on trapped insects and resident bugs.
care.propagation: Seed (difficult) or cuttings.
care.problems: Root rot, low humidity, loss of resident insects, scale.

genera.nativeRange: Eastern and south-eastern North America, from Canada to Florida and Texas
genera.description: Sarracenia pitchers are tall, hollow leaves with a nectar-secreting rim, a slippery interior and downward-pointing hairs that guide insects to a digestive pool at the base. The genus includes the purple pitcher plant, the tall yellow trumpets and the hooded, nodding pitchers of Sarracenia psittacina. They are among the easiest and most rewarding carnivores for a sunny bog garden.
genera.identification: Hollow, tubular or hooded pitchers arising from a rhizome, with a wing along the front and a lid or hood. Flowers are large, nodding and bizarre.
genera.ecology: They grow in nutrient-poor pine savannas, bogs and seepages that depend on fire and clean water. Habitat loss and poaching have made several species rare.

care.overview: Full sun, wet feet and a cold winter dormancy. Perfect for an outdoor bog garden in a temperate climate.
care.light: Full sun; at least six hours of direct sun.
care.water: Stand in 2–10 cm of mineral-free water during growth. Keep the bog wet year-round.
care.soil: Peat : sand or perlite 1:1. Never use potting soil or fertiliser.
care.temperature: Temperate; most species are hardy with mulch or a sheltered bog.
care.dormancy: Cold winter dormancy is essential. Keep cool and moist, not warm and wet.
care.feeding: Outdoor plants catch their own insects. Do not fertilise.
care.propagation: Rhizome division in late winter; seed (slow).
care.problems: Rot in stagnant water, scale, aphids, squirrel and slug damage.

genera.nativeRange: Tropical West Africa: Sierra Leone, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire
genera.description: Triphyophyllum peltatum is a remarkable tropical liana and one of the few plants known to be a facultative carnivore. In its juvenile phase it produces sticky, glandular leaves that trap insects; later it switches to ordinary leaves and a climbing habit. It is not a practical cultivated plant.
genera.identification: A large forest liana with three leaf types: glandular carnivorous leaves, ordinary leaves and hooked climbing leaves.
genera.ecology: It grows in tropical rainforest in West Africa. The carnivorous phase is thought to help the plant acquire nutrients during rapid early growth.

care.overview: Not recommended for cultivation. It needs tropical rainforest conditions and a large climbing structure.
care.water: High humidity and evenly moist, free-draining soil.
care.soil: Humus-rich tropical mix.
care.dormancy: None.
care.feeding: Not applicable in cultivation.
care.propagation: Seed or cuttings, with difficulty.
care.problems: Not a houseplant; leave wild plants undisturbed.

genera.nativeRange: Cosmopolitan, on every continent except Antarctica, with centres of diversity in South America and Australia
genera.description: Utricularia is the largest genus of carnivorous plants, with more than 240 accepted species. Its traps are tiny, hollow bladders that suck in water and prey when a trigger hair is touched, one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom. Bladderworts grow as aquatics, terrestrials, epiphytes and even in wet sand.
genera.identification: Bladder-like traps on the stems, stolons or leaves; flowers are usually yellow, violet or white on tall scapes. Aquatic species may look like loose threads or floating mats.
genera.ecology: They occupy an extraordinary range of nutrient-poor wetlands, from acid bogs and lakes to wet cliffs and bromeliad tanks. Many are tiny and easily overlooked.

care.overview: The care group matters: aquatic, terrestrial or epiphytic. All want mineral-free water, bright light and a nutrient-poor mix.
care.water: Mineral-free water. Aquatics float or are anchored in shallow water; terrestrials stand in a tray.
care.soil: Aquatics need no soil; terrestrials use peat : sand : perlite; epiphytes use sphagnum or tree-fern fibre.
care.temperature: Depends on the species; most are warm-temperate to tropical.
care.dormancy: Aquatics may form turions; terrestrials may die back to a resting bud.
care.feeding: Do not feed; the traps capture microfauna.
care.propagation: Division, stolons, turions, seed.
care.problems: Algae, drying out, hard water, aphids and rot.

aquatic.label: Aquatic
aquatic.water: Soft, acidic water; keep the plants submerged or floating.
aquatic.soil: No soil; use a shallow tray or pond.
aquatic.notes: Grow in shallow, sunlit water with no fish. Winter turions form in cold conditions.

terrestrial.label: Terrestrial
terrestrial.water: Stand in 1–2 cm of mineral-free water.
terrestrial.notes: The easiest bladderworts. Many spread into a carpet and flower freely.

epiphytic.label: Epiphytic
epiphytic.water: High humidity; mist regularly and keep the mount moist.
epiphytic.notes: Tropical epiphytes for a terrarium or orchid house. Excellent airflow is essential.

careGroups.label: Temperate bog
careGroups.tagline: Cold winters, wet summers and full sun.
careGroups.description: The classic hardy carnivore group: North American pitcher plants, Venus flytraps, thread-leaved sundews and hardy butterworts. These plants expect a pronounced winter dormancy, a permanently wet, acidic substrate and as much direct sun as the growing season can provide. In mild climates they can live outdoors all year; in colder or warmer climates the challenge is protecting the roots from hard freezes while still giving the plant a real winter.
careGroups.light: Full sun outdoors for at least six hours a day. Indoors, use a powerful full-spectrum LED close to the plant.
careGroups.water: Stand the pot in 2–5 cm of rainwater, distilled water or reverse-osmosis water. Keep the mix wet throughout growth. Reduce to just damp during the coldest weeks, but never let the root zone dry completely.
careGroups.soil: A 1:1 mix of peat moss and coarse silica sand or perlite. Some growers add a little live sphagnum on the surface. Avoid compost, loam and fertiliser.
careGroups.temperature: Warm summers and cool winters. Most species tolerate light frost when dormant, but protect the pots from hard, prolonged freezes.
careGroups.dormancy: Essential. Short days and cold temperatures trigger resting buds, dieback or a slow-down. Do not keep temperate plants warm and actively growing through winter.
careGroups.feeding: Let them catch their own insects outdoors. Do not add fertiliser to the soil. A very occasional foliar feed at quarter strength is controversial and rarely necessary.
careGroups.propagation: Division in late winter or early spring, seed, leaf cuttings for sundews, and rhizome division for pitcher plants.
careGroups.problems: Hard water, drying out, warm winter conditions, aphids, botrytis in still air, and squirrels or birds digging in the bog.
tips: Use a large container so the root mass stays cool and evenly wet.
Rainwater is not optional; hard tap water slowly poisons the substrate.
Give pitcher plants a winter check for rot and remove dead growth in early spring.

careGroups.label: Subtropical rosette
careGroups.tagline: Forgiving, frost-sensitive and happy in a bright window.
careGroups.description: Warm-temperate and subtropical rosette sundews, including the Cape sundew and its relatives. They grow quickly, flower freely and tolerate a wide range of conditions as long as the roots stay wet and the light is strong. They do not need a hard winter dormancy, but growth slows in cool, short days.
careGroups.light: Full sun to very bright light. A south-facing windowsill or a strong LED works well. Weak light produces pale, stretched leaves.
careGroups.water: Stand in 1–3 cm of mineral-free water. Keep the tray topped up; these plants dislike drying out.
careGroups.soil: Peat : perlite or peat : silica sand at 1:1. A little live sphagnum on top helps keep humidity high.
careGroups.temperature: Warm to mild: roughly 15–30°C. Protect from frost. Indoors they cope with normal room temperatures.
careGroups.dormancy: No hard dormancy. Growth slows in winter; reduce water slightly but do not let the mix dry out.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches small insects. Do not fertilise. If grown indoors without insects, a tiny amount of dried bloodworm or a very dilute foliar feed can help, but it is easy to overdo.
careGroups.propagation: Leaf cuttings in water or on wet peat, division, and fresh seed. Many species self-seed.
careGroups.problems: Hard water, mineral build-up, aphids, thrips, and rot when air is stagnant and the mix is too dense.
tips: Repot every one to two years to remove mineral build-up.
A small fan improves airflow indoors and reduces mould.
Remove flower stalks if you want the plant to put energy into leaves.

careGroups.label: Cape winter-growing
careGroups.tagline: Wet winters, dry summers and a Mediterranean rhythm.
careGroups.description: South African winter-rainfall sundews that grow during the cool, wet months and retreat underground or into a resting rosette during the hot, dry summer. The dry summer rest is not optional: keeping these plants wet year-round is the most common reason they fail in cultivation.
careGroups.light: Full sun during the winter growing season. Keep the rosette compact and colourful.
careGroups.water: Wet during winter growth. In late spring, stop watering and let the substrate dry out as the plant goes dormant. Resume watering when new growth appears in autumn.
careGroups.soil: A very open, sandy mix: peat : coarse sand : perlite at 1:2:1. Excellent drainage is essential.
careGroups.temperature: Cool and mild in winter; hot and dry in summer. Protect from hard frost and from cold, wet summer conditions.
careGroups.dormancy: Long, dry summer dormancy. Some species die back to a tuber or corm; others form a small resting rosette.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches during the growing season. Do not feed during dormancy.
careGroups.propagation: Seed, division, and tuber or corm separation.
careGroups.problems: Summer rot, hard water, insufficient light, and premature watering after dormancy.
tips: Mark the pot and keep it completely dry but shaded in summer.
Use deep pots for tuberous and corm-forming species.
Start watering only when you see new growth, not on a fixed calendar date.

careGroups.label: Pygmy sundew
careGroups.tagline: Tiny rosettes, jewel-like colour and gemmae.
careGroups.description: A group of small Australian sundews with compact rosettes and spectacular colour under strong light. They grow through the cool, wet season and survive the dry season as seed or resting buds. Many produce gemmae — tiny leaf-like propagules — in autumn, making them easy to share and propagate.
careGroups.light: Full sun. Strong light keeps the rosettes tight and brings out red, bronze and gold colour.
careGroups.water: Wet during winter growth, then gradually drier in summer. Do not keep the substrate soggy through hot nights.
careGroups.soil: Very sandy peat: peat : coarse sand at 1:3, with a little perlite. Low nutrient content is important.
careGroups.temperature: Cool to mild. Hot, humid nights are more dangerous than dry heat.
careGroups.dormancy: Dry summer dormancy. Many plants die back to a small bud; gemmae may remain dormant in the substrate.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches tiny insects. Do not feed with anything large enough to damage the rosette.
careGroups.propagation: Gemmae in autumn is the easiest method. Sow them on the surface of wet sandy peat and keep them cool and bright.
careGroups.problems: Damping-off, algae, heat, aphids and disturbance of the shallow roots.
tips: Use shallow pots with a very sandy surface.
Sow gemmae immediately; they lose viability quickly.
Keep the pot cool and airy after gemmae germinate.

careGroups.label: Tuberous sundew
careGroups.tagline: Underground tubers, winter growth and a long dry rest.
careGroups.description: Australian tuberous sundews that disappear underground for the hot, dry summer and emerge with the winter rains. Some form climbing stems; others stay close to the ground. The tuber is the plant's survival organ, and the dry rest is the key to keeping it healthy.
careGroups.light: Full sun during the growing season. Climbing species benefit from a small trellis.
careGroups.water: Wet during winter growth. Stop watering as the leaves yellow in spring. Keep the pot completely dry through summer, then resume watering when the first shoots appear in autumn.
careGroups.soil: Deep, very sandy mix: peat : coarse sand : perlite at 1:2:1. The pot must drain freely.
careGroups.temperature: Cool and mild in winter. Protect from hard frost and from hot, wet conditions.
careGroups.dormancy: Long, completely dry summer dormancy. Tubers can remain dormant for months.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches during growth. Never feed during dormancy.
careGroups.propagation: Seed, tuber division, and leaf cuttings for some species. Tubers should be handled carefully.
careGroups.problems: Rot from summer watering, shallow pots, hard water, and early watering before shoots appear.
tips: Use pots at least 15–20 cm deep.
Store dormant pots dry and shaded, not cold and damp.
Label the pot: the tuber is invisible for much of the year.

careGroups.label: Petiolaris complex
careGroups.description: A challenging group of tropical Australian sundews with hairy leaves and a pronounced wet-season growth spurt. In the wild they experience a hot, humid wet season followed by a dry season, when many die back to a hairy resting bud. Recreating that rhythm is the key to growing them well.
careGroups.light: Very bright, hot light. Strong light is essential for healthy, compact growth.
careGroups.water: Wet during the wet season. During the dry-season rest, reduce water and keep the substrate only barely moist.
careGroups.soil: Sandy peat with excellent drainage: peat : coarse sand : perlite at 1:2:1.
careGroups.temperature: Hot: roughly 25–35°C during growth. Warm nights and high humidity help.
careGroups.dormancy: Dry-season dormancy. Plants may lose their leaves and retreat to a hairy resting bud.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches. Do not overfeed; the leaves are sensitive.
careGroups.propagation: Seed, leaf cuttings and division of resting buds.
careGroups.problems: Cold, wet roots, rot, spider mites in dry air, and failure to break dormancy.
tips: Keep the root zone warm even in winter.
Do not panic when the plant dies back; keep the resting bud barely moist.
Give the plant a real dry-season reduction, not constant wetness.

careGroups.label: Annual
careGroups.description: Short-lived carnivores that complete their life cycle in a single season and survive the rest of the year as seed. Annual sundews, rainbow plants and some bladderworts fit here. The trick is to sow fresh seed, keep the seedlings warm and bright, and let the colony self-seed for the next generation.
careGroups.light: Full sun to very bright light. Seedlings stretch badly in low light.
careGroups.water: Keep the surface wet while plants are growing. Use a shallow tray and mineral-free water.
careGroups.soil: Sandy peat: peat : coarse sand at 1:1 or 1:2. The surface should stay open and bright.
careGroups.dormancy: None. The plant dies after flowering and seeding; the seeds carry the next generation.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches tiny insects. Do not fertilise.
careGroups.propagation: Fresh seed sown on the surface of wet substrate. Many species self-seed if allowed to flower.
careGroups.problems: Damping-off, algae, seed predation, and losing the colony because the last plants were not allowed to set seed.
tips: Sow small amounts every few weeks for a continuous display.
Let at least one plant self-seed before removing it.
Keep the pot humid but airy; still, warm air invites damping-off.

careGroups.label: Woody perennial
careGroups.tagline: Deep roots, strong light and a dry-season rest.
careGroups.description: Long-lived, woody or rootstock-forming carnivores such as the perennial rainbow plants. They invest in a deep root system and can live for many years, but they resent root disturbance and need a pronounced dry-season rest. Deep pots and patience are the main requirements.
careGroups.light: Full sun to very bright light.
careGroups.water: Wet during growth; reduce water during the dry-season rest. Do not let the rootstock stay soggy when the plant is dormant.
careGroups.soil: Deep, sandy peat with excellent drainage. A mix of peat, coarse sand and perlite works well.
careGroups.temperature: Warm to mild. Protect from frost.
careGroups.dormancy: Dry-season rest. The plant may die back to a woody rootstock.
careGroups.propagation: Seed or careful division of the rootstock. Avoid disturbing established plants.
careGroups.problems: Root rot, transplant shock, hard water and insufficient light.
tips: Use the deepest pot you can accommodate.
Do not repot unless the plant is actively growing.
Reduce water, not light, during the resting season.

careGroups.label: Mediterranean
careGroups.tagline: Winter growth, summer drought and brilliant light.
careGroups.description: Species from Mediterranean-climate regions, including the Portuguese dewy pine and the South African Roridula. They grow through the cooler, wetter months and endure a hot, dry summer. Excellent drainage and a dry summer rest are more important than rich soil.
careGroups.light: Full sun, all day if possible.
careGroups.water: Water during active growth, then reduce sharply in summer. Cephalotus prefers evenly moist roots; Drosophyllum and Roridula need a drier, very well-drained root zone.
careGroups.soil: A very open, mineral mix. For Drosophyllum, use coarse sand, perlite and a little peat or leaf mould. For Cephalotus, a sandy peat mix with good drainage.
careGroups.temperature: Cool to warm, with a pronounced seasonal rhythm. Protect from hard frost.
careGroups.dormancy: Summer dormancy or slow-down. Keep the plants dry-ish and well ventilated.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches. Drosophyllum and Roridula are sensitive to root disturbance and fertiliser.
careGroups.propagation: Seed for Drosophyllum (sow fresh, dislike transplanting); division or seed for Cephalotus; seed or cuttings for Roridula.
careGroups.problems: Root rot, summer humidity, transplant shock and hard water.
tips: Sow Drosophyllum in its final pot; it hates being moved.
Use a gritty top dressing to keep the crown dry.
Give Cephalotus cool roots and strong light for the best colour.

careGroups.label: Mexican butterwort
careGroups.description: Mexican Pinguicula are famous for their two seasonal forms: sticky, carnivorous summer rosettes and tight, succulent winter rosettes. They grow on limestone cliffs and seepages, so they tolerate a slightly alkaline mix and need a dry winter rest. The winter rosette is not dead — it is waiting.
careGroups.light: Bright, filtered light to full sun. Indoors, a bright windowsill or LED is ideal.
careGroups.water: Wet during summer growth. In winter, let the mix dry almost completely and water only enough to keep the succulent rosette from shrivelling.
careGroups.soil: A loose mix of peat, perlite and vermiculite, with a little coarse sand. Some growers add crushed limestone or use a slightly alkaline mix.
careGroups.temperature: Warm days and cooler nights. Protect from frost; winter rosettes tolerate cool, dry conditions.
careGroups.dormancy: Dry winter dormancy with a small, non-carnivorous rosette. Resume watering when carnivorous leaves appear.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches small insects. Do not fertilise the roots.
careGroups.propagation: Leaf cuttings, division, and seed. Winter rosettes can be separated carefully.
careGroups.problems: Rot from wet winters, hard water, aphids, and scorching in sudden full sun.
tips: Mark the calendar: the winter rosette needs less water, not more.
Use rainwater; Mexican butterworts are sensitive to minerals.
Leaf cuttings root readily on the surface of damp perlite.

careGroups.label: Tropical butterwort
careGroups.description: Warm-climate Pinguicula from the Neotropics, including epiphytic and lithophytic species. They lack a hard dormancy and prefer steady warmth, high humidity and a loose, airy root zone. Good airflow is as important as water.
careGroups.light: Bright, filtered light. Avoid harsh midday sun through glass.
careGroups.water: Keep moist year-round, but never waterlogged. Use mineral-free water.
careGroups.soil: Loose, humus-rich epiphytic mix: peat, perlite, orchid bark and a little sphagnum.
careGroups.temperature: Warm year-round: roughly 18–28°C. Protect from cold draughts.
careGroups.dormancy: None. Growth may slow slightly in cool weather.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches. A very light foliar feed can help in low-insect environments, but avoid overfeeding.
careGroups.problems: Rot, fungus gnats, low humidity, and cold, wet roots.
tips: Grow on a humidity tray or in a well-ventilated terrarium.
Keep the crown above the substrate line.
Inspect the rosette centre for mould after cool, damp spells.

careGroups.label: Lowland tropical pitcher
careGroups.tagline: Warm nights, high humidity and steady heat.
careGroups.description: Tropical pitcher plants from low elevations, where nights stay warm and humidity is high. They grow quickly in the right conditions but struggle in cool houses. The main challenge is maintaining warmth at night without sacrificing light and airflow.
careGroups.light: Bright, filtered light. Some direct morning sun is fine; protect from scorching midday sun.
careGroups.water: Keep the mix evenly moist, never soggy. Use mineral-free water. High humidity is important, but the roots still need air.
careGroups.soil: An open epiphytic mix: long-fibre sphagnum, orchid bark, perlite and charcoal. Avoid dense peat.
careGroups.temperature: Day 25–32°C; night 20–23°C. Avoid drops below about 18°C.
careGroups.dormancy: None. Growth slows slightly in cooler weather.
careGroups.feeding: Feed pitchers occasionally with a tiny amount of fish food or dried insects. Do not fertilise the roots.
careGroups.propagation: Stem cuttings, basal shoots, and seed. Cuttings root well in live sphagnum.
careGroups.problems: Cold nights, root rot, spider mites in dry air, and pitcher loss after repotting.
tips: Use a thermometer at night, not just during the day.
Keep the plant warm but move air around it.
Do not trim healthy pitchers; they are the plant's food source.

careGroups.label: Highland cloud forest
careGroups.tagline: Cool nights, bright days and cloud-forest humidity.
careGroups.description: Pitcher plants from montane and cloud-forest habitats, where days are mild and nights are distinctly cool. The night temperature drop is the defining requirement. Highland species are often slower-growing but long-lived, and many produce spectacular upper pitchers.
careGroups.light: Bright, filtered light. High-altitude species appreciate strong light with cool roots.
careGroups.water: Keep the mix moist and very airy. Use mineral-free water and never let the root zone stagnate.
careGroups.soil: Long-fibre sphagnum, orchid bark, perlite and a little charcoal. Keep it open and acidic.
careGroups.temperature: Day 18–26°C; night 10–16°C. The night drop is essential, especially for ultra-highland species.
careGroups.dormancy: None, but growth slows in winter. Do not force growth with heat.
careGroups.feeding: Feed pitchers sparingly. Highlanders are slow-growing and easy to overfeed.
careGroups.propagation: Stem cuttings, basal shoots, and seed. Cuttings need cool conditions and high humidity.
careGroups.problems: Warm nights, root rot, sudden humidity crashes, and stress after shipping.
tips: Measure night temperature; it matters more than day temperature.
Use a cool cellar, greenhouse or terrarium with active night cooling.
Keep the plant in the same spot; highlanders dislike being moved.

careGroups.label: Intermediate tropical pitcher
careGroups.description: The broad middle group of tropical pitcher plants and hybrids that tolerate ordinary warm-temperate conditions. Many popular garden hybrids are intermediate and will grow well in a bright conservatory or terrarium with warm days and mildly cool nights. It is the best starting point for most new Nepenthes growers.
careGroups.light: Bright, filtered light with some direct sun. Protect from hot midday glare.
careGroups.water: Keep the mix moist but airy. Use mineral-free water and allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings.
careGroups.soil: Long-fibre sphagnum, orchid bark, perlite and charcoal in roughly equal parts.
careGroups.temperature: Day 22–30°C; night 16–20°C. A modest night drop is beneficial.
careGroups.dormancy: None. Growth may slow in winter.
careGroups.feeding: Feed pitchers occasionally with small insects or fish food. Do not fertilise the roots.
careGroups.propagation: Stem cuttings, basal shoots, and seed.
careGroups.problems: Root rot, low humidity, spider mites, and pitcher loss after a sudden change in conditions.
tips: Choose a hybrid rather than a fussy species for your first pitcher plant.
Keep the substrate open and the air moving.
Do not panic if the plant drops its pitchers after moving; new ones will follow.

careGroups.label: Aquatic bladderwort
careGroups.tagline: Float, submerge and let the bladders hunt.
careGroups.description: Free-floating or submerged bladderworts and the waterwheel plant. They capture tiny aquatic invertebrates with suction traps and need soft, acidic, mineral-free water. The main enemies are algae, fish, hard water and overheating.
careGroups.light: Full sun to bright light. A shallow outdoor tub is ideal in summer.
careGroups.water: Soft, acidic, mineral-free water. Keep the water clean and moving gently. Avoid hard tap water entirely.
careGroups.soil: No soil. Float the plants, or anchor them lightly to a mesh or a little live sphagnum.
careGroups.temperature: Warm in summer; cool in winter. Some species form turions and die back.
careGroups.dormancy: Cool winter rest or turion formation for temperate species. Tropical species may grow year-round.
careGroups.feeding: They catch their own aquatic microfauna. Do not add fish food or fertiliser to the water.
careGroups.propagation: Division of floating stems, turions, and seed.
careGroups.problems: Algae, duckweed competition, fish and snails, hard water, and summer overheating.
tips: Use a wide, shallow container with a lid of shade cloth to limit algae.
Keep fish out; they eat the plants and the prey.
Harvest a few stems before winter in case the main colony collapses.

careGroups.label: Terrestrial bladderwort
careGroups.tagline: Wet soil, tiny bladders and surprising flowers.
careGroups.description: The easiest bladderworts, growing in wet, sandy peat and catching microscopic soil life with underground bladders. Many spread into a dense carpet and reward growers with orchid-like flowers. They are ideal for a sunny bog tray or a terrarium shelf.
careGroups.light: Bright light to full sun. Flowering is much better with strong light.
careGroups.water: Stand in 1–2 cm of mineral-free water. Keep the substrate consistently wet but not stagnant.
careGroups.soil: Peat : coarse sand : perlite at 1:1:1. A little live sphagnum on the surface helps.
careGroups.temperature: Warm to mild. Protect from frost unless the species is temperate.
careGroups.dormancy: Many species slow down or die back in winter; some form small tubers or resting buds.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches soil microfauna. Do not fertilise.
careGroups.propagation: Division, stolon cuttings, and seed. Fragments establish easily.
careGroups.problems: Algae, moss overgrowth, drying out, and fungus gnats.
tips: Keep the colony slightly crowded; bladderworts seem to grow better that way.
Top-dress with live sphagnum to maintain humidity.
Flower spikes are worth the wait; avoid moving the pot while buds are developing.

careGroups.label: Epiphytic bladderwort
careGroups.tagline: Tree-dwelling specialists for the orchid house.
careGroups.description: Tropical Utricularia from cloud forests and tree trunks, including some of the most spectacular species in the genus. They grow in live sphagnum or on tree-fern fibre and demand high humidity, excellent airflow and cool, stable conditions. These are not beginner plants.
careGroups.light: Bright, filtered light. Protect from hot direct sun.
careGroups.water: High humidity; mist regularly and keep the mount or moss moist. Use mineral-free water.
careGroups.soil: Live sphagnum or tree-fern fibre on a mount, or a very open epiphytic mix in a basket.
careGroups.temperature: Cool to warm, depending on species; many highland species need a night drop.
careGroups.dormancy: None, but growth slows in cool or dry periods.
careGroups.feeding: Self-catches microfauna. Do not fertilise; epiphytes are sensitive to salts.
careGroups.propagation: Division of stolons, careful cuttings, and seed.
careGroups.problems: Desiccation, rot in still air, spider mites, and sudden collapse after shipping.
tips: Mount the plant at an angle so water drains away from the crown.
Use a fan; high humidity without airflow is a rot trap.
Keep a backup division in a different spot.

entries.title: Database baseline published
entries.summary: Initial snapshot of 751 accepted species and natural hybrids across 21 genera, compiled from the ICPS Carnivorous Plant Names Resource. Every accepted name on the 21 genus pages was captured, including natural hybrids and nested infraspecific taxa.

entries.title: Nine recent descriptions added to the watchlist
entries.summary: Recent species accepted in the primary literature but not yet present in the ICPS snapshot are shown as provisional entries. They are excluded from the 751 ICPS count and are promoted automatically when ICPS lists them.

entries.title: All 939 ICPS-registered cultivars added
entries.summary: The catalogue now covers every cultivar on the ICPS registered-cultivar list, not just Dionaea: 939 records across Byblis, Cephalotus, Darlingtonia, Dionaea, Drosera, Heliamphora, Nepenthes, Pinguicula, Sarracenia and Utricularia. Each record carries the registration date, authority, originator, registrant, publication, standard, etymology and parent formula where the register records them, plus parent care and native range. Ten cultivars have a verified cultivar-specific open-licensed photograph; the other 929 use a clearly labelled representative parent-species image. Cultivars remain excluded from wild-species counts, country totals and range maps.

entries.title: Collection and wishlist, stored on your device
entries.summary: Every species and cultivar page can now be added to a personal collection or wishlist. Both lists live in this browser's local storage only, never in the database, and can be printed or exported as JSON. The catalogue itself stays read-only: only maintainers can change names, care notes or photographs. Old favourites are migrated into the collection automatically.

entries.title: Monthly ICPS check automated
entries.summary: A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow now refreshes the ICPS species and cultivar snapshots on the first day of every month, diffs them against the catalogue, adds new names, records the result in data/icps-check.json, and rebuilds and deploys the site. The same check can be run locally with node scripts/check-icps.mjs.

watchlist.note: Curated watchlist of recently published carnivorous-plant species that are accepted in the primary literature but were not present in the 9 November 2026 ICPS Carnivorous Plant Names Resource snapshot. These are shown as provisional entries, clearly distinguished from the 751 ICPS-accepted taxa. The list is not exhaustive; the updater promotes names automatically once ICPS lists them.

taxa.name: Drosera magnifica
taxa.typeLocality: Pico do Padre Ângelo, eastern Minas Gerais, Brazil

originPoints.label: Pico do Padre Ângelo, Minas Gerais (approx.)

taxa.summary: One of the largest sundews in the world, discovered through photographs posted on Facebook and described from a single mountain top in Minas Gerais.
taxa.description: Drosera magnifica is a giant sundew with a climbing or scrambling stem that can exceed a metre, long dewy leaves and a candelabrum-like inflorescence. It is known from a single mountain top in eastern Minas Gerais, where it grows among sandstone outcrops. The species was described in 2015 after photographs taken by an orchid hunter were recognised as an undescribed sundew, making it one of the first plants discovered through social media.
taxa.etymology: magnifica means 'magnificent', referring to the plant's striking size and appearance.
taxa.discoveredBy: Recognised from photographs posted on Facebook by Reginaldo Vasconcelos and described by Fernando Rivadavia and Paulo Gonella.
taxa.careNotes: Treat as a warm-temperate to subtropical sundew with a very open, sandy mix and strong light. It is large and vigorous in cultivation but has a tiny wild range; propagation material should be traceable and never wild-collected.
taxa.conservationNote: Assessed as Critically Endangered in the protologue. Its single known locality is vulnerable to fire, mining and habitat clearance.

taxa.name: Nepenthes pongoides
taxa.typeLocality: Meliau Range, central Sabah, Borneo, Malaysia
taxa.summary: A recently described giant lowland pitcher plant from an ultramafic peak in Sabah, known from only two subpopulations.
taxa.description: Nepenthes pongoides is one of the largest Nepenthes described in recent years, with a massive rosette, peltate tendril insertion and a dense, persistent covering of long reddish hairs. It is known from the low-elevation Meliau Range in central Sabah, where only a few dozen mature individuals have been observed. The species was formally described in 2024 and assessed as Critically Endangered.
taxa.etymology: The epithet refers to the orangutan (Pongo), reflecting the plant's reddish, hairy appearance.
taxa.discoveredBy: Described by Alviana Damit, S. Yusof, J. Jumian and Alastair S. Robinson in 2024.
taxa.careNotes: A warm lowland species. Provide steady warmth, high humidity, bright filtered light and an open epiphytic mix. It is not yet widely established in cultivation.
taxa.conservationNote: Known from two subpopulations and assessed as Critically Endangered. Habitat protection is the priority; horticultural material is extremely limited.

taxa.name: Nepenthes kampalili
taxa.typeLocality: Mt. Kampalili, Maragusan, Davao de Oro, Mindanao, Philippines
taxa.summary: A montane pitcher plant from the limestone karst forests of eastern Mindanao, described in 2024.
taxa.description: Nepenthes kampalili belongs to section Villosa and grows in the limestone karst bonsai forest of the eastern Mindanao biodiversity corridor. It differs from close relatives in its densely pubescent ground pitchers and lid, and in details of the tendril and spur. The species was assessed as Critically Endangered in its description.
taxa.discoveredBy: Described by Noel E. Lagunday, Aimanuelzon P. Yorong and Victor B. Amoroso in 2024.
taxa.careNotes: A highland species: cool nights, high humidity and very open, airy roots. Treat as an advanced collection plant until cultivation is better documented.
taxa.conservationNote: Assessed as Critically Endangered, with poaching and habitat loss identified as the main threats.

taxa.name: Nepenthes higaonon
taxa.summary: A 2025 species from the gravel substrates of northern Mindanao, assessed as Critically Endangered.
taxa.description: Nepenthes higaonon is a climbing pitcher plant in section Alatae, known from the gravel substrates of northern Mindanao. It is similar to N. viridis but differs in leaf attachment, leaf shape, venation, pitcher shape and inflorescence structure. The species was described in 2025 and assessed as Critically Endangered.
taxa.discoveredBy: Described by Noel E. Lagunday, Melbert James G. Baul, Ramil P. Ansihagan and Victor B. Amoroso in 2025.
taxa.careNotes: Warm lowland conditions, bright filtered light and an open mix. Newly described species should be treated as conservation material, not a commodity.
taxa.conservationNote: Faces poaching, shifting cultivation and habitat loss, with no legislative protection at the type locality.

taxa.name: Nepenthes maagnawense
taxa.typeLocality: Mt. Maagnaw, Kitanglad Range, Bukidnon, Mindanao, Philippines, 2300–2700 m
taxa.summary: A high-elevation pitcher plant from the Kitanglad Range, described in 2025 and assessed as Endangered.
taxa.description: Nepenthes maagnawense grows in shrubland at 2300–2700 m on Mt. Maagnaw in the Kitanglad Range. It is a member of section Alatae and differs from N. kitanglad in stem shape, venation, pitcher proportions and lid appendage. The species is known only from the type locality and is estimated to number fewer than 250 mature individuals.
taxa.discoveredBy: Described by Noel E. Lagunday and Victor B. Amoroso in 2025.
taxa.careNotes: A true highland species. Cool nights, strong light, high humidity and excellent drainage are essential. It is not a beginner plant.
taxa.conservationNote: Assessed as Endangered, with a population of fewer than 250 mature individuals and a very restricted range.

taxa.name: Nepenthes megastoma
taxa.typeLocality: Mount Saint Paul karst, Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park, Palawan, Philippines, c. 250 m
taxa.summary: A micro-endemic pitcher plant from vertical limestone walls in Palawan, described in 2025.
taxa.description: Nepenthes megastoma is known from three locations on vertical limestone walls in the Mount Saint Paul karst formation on Palawan. It has highly branched stems, campanulate pitchers, peltate tendril insertion and dimorphic upper pitchers. The species is assessed as Critically Endangered and appears to be closely related to the Palawan endemic N. philippinensis.
taxa.discoveredBy: Described by Alastair S. Robinson, R. Bustamante and Charles Altomonte in 2025.
taxa.careNotes: A warm, humid lowland species from limestone. It is not established in general cultivation and should be treated as a conservation-sensitive plant.
taxa.conservationNote: Known from three subpopulations with few individuals; fire, typhoons and poaching are immediate threats.

taxa.name: Nepenthes candalaga
taxa.authors: Lagunday, Dela Rosa, Cleofei, Patano, Coritico & Amoroso
taxa.typeLocality: Mt. Candalaga, Maragusan, Davao de Oro, Mindanao, Philippines, 1800–2100 m
taxa.summary: A montane pitcher plant from Mt. Candalaga in eastern Mindanao, described in 2022.
taxa.description: Nepenthes candalaga is a member of section Alatae from the tropical upper montane forest of Mt. Candalaga. It resembles N. justinae but differs in leaf venation, lid shape, spur tip, lid appendage, trap wings and the upper pitcher rim. The species was assessed as Critically Endangered.
taxa.discoveredBy: Described by Noel E. Lagunday and colleagues in 2022.
taxa.careNotes: Highland conditions with cool nights and high humidity. It is a conservation-sensitive species with a very small known range.
taxa.conservationNote: Assessed as Critically Endangered; deforestation and habitat loss are the main threats.

taxa.name: Nepenthes nebularum
taxa.typeLocality: south-eastern Mindanao, Philippines, up to 1800 m
taxa.summary: A highland pitcher plant from south-eastern Mindanao, closely related to N. truncata and N. robcantleyi.
taxa.description: Nepenthes nebularum is a highland species from mossy forest in south-eastern Mindanao, recorded with certainty from only a few mountains. It has a dense, woolly reddish indumentum on the petiole wings, tendrils and traps, and is closely related to N. truncata and N. robcantleyi. Its conservation status has been treated as Data Deficient.
taxa.discoveredBy: Described by Geoff Mansell and Wally Suarez in 2016.
taxa.careNotes: Cool highland conditions, high humidity and an open epiphytic mix. It can be grown as an epiphyte or lithophyte.
taxa.conservationNote: Data Deficient; its small known range and montane habitat make it vulnerable to collection and habitat loss.

taxa.name: Nepenthes maximoides
taxa.summary: A possibly extinct pitcher plant known from a single herbarium specimen collected more than a century ago.
taxa.description: Nepenthes maximoides is known from a single historical specimen from Luzon, probably collected on Mt. Banahaw, and had not been recorded for about 110 years when it was described in 2020. Its large, narrowly funnel-shaped upper pitchers and unusual lid appendages resemble those of N. maxima, a striking case of convergent evolution. It is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct).
taxa.discoveredBy: Recognised in herbarium material by Charles King and Martin Cheek and described in 2020.
taxa.careNotes: Not known in cultivation. Any material would be of extreme conservation value; do not expect this species in the horticultural trade.
taxa.conservationNote: Assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct). The only known specimen is historical, and the suspected type locality has been heavily disturbed.
